articles.title: You can see You Can See Everything everywhere
articles.summary: The documentary You Can See Everything about Elizabeth Holmes is a box-office hit, an awards season contender and a social media obsession.

image.caption: This composite shows Jimmy Fallon, from left, and Jamie Lee Curtis on The Tonight Show parodying Nathan Fielder and Elizbeth Holmes from the film, You Can See Everything. (NBC/A24)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
The documentary You Can See Everything about Elizabeth Holmes is a box-office hit, an awards season contender and a social media obsession.
Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos founder and convicted fraudster, has become a meme machine
Some movies leave you with a memorable line. You Can See Everything leaves you with a face inches from yours and plenty of parodies.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's movie about Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos founder and convicted fraudster, has become a meme machine, powered by the film's most unnerving visual signature: close talking. Online, the answer has been to turn the pauses, the proximity, the dead-serious eye contact and that discomfort into a format.

items: You Can See Everything sells out theatres, and people can't stop talking about it
Loved You Can See Everything? Thank Canada

blocks.text: The latest take came on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon, where Jamie Lee Curtis played Holmes and Fallon took on Fielder. They delivered a shot-for-shot remake of of one of the film's most intense exchanges.

With tense music underneath, Fallon mirrored Fielder's measured questions and subtle expressions while Curtis held Holmes's wide-eyed stare and repeated her lines, including, "I'm engaging with you as a human being." The pair stayed in character until Fallon walked away and Curtis broke the tension.
The spoof quickly won over viewers online, with fans calling it Emmy-worthy and some saying Fallon looked so much like Fielder they briefly thought it was him.
This Hour Has 22 Minutes borrows the film's close-talking tension for a parody negotiation between U.S. President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney.
As Trump insists he isn't lying, Carney asks, "So you won't try to make Canada the 51st state?"
Trump promises he won't, then admits, "I lied."
Their face-to-face exchange spirals into an absurd argument about truth and trust, with Carney struggling to follow Trump's shifting story.

The joke made its way to Washington Square Park in New York City, where dozens gathered for a Holmes and Fielder lookalike contest. Organized by comedian Maddy West and a friend, the event drew more than 200 registration responses.

The winners were Nicole Travolta, an actor and comedian who has been impersonating Holmes since 2022, and Joe Sivick, whose resemblance to Fielder was convincing enough to briefly fool one of the organizers.
Fans react online

On platforms including X, Instagram, TikTok and Reddit, users have also been reacting to Holmes and Fielder's real-life exchanges, even making parodies of their own. One Reddit user reimagined the film as You Can Eat Anything.
Other memes transplant the film's dead-serious dialogue into everyday situations. One X user posted, "It's finally fall, we're going apple picking with my college friends next Sunday at 1 pm."
A user on Reddit re-shared this one, which said, "My cat telling me she hasn't been fed yet. Why would I deceive you? There's no reason for me to do that."
A reddit user re-shared this meme that says, 'My cat telling me she hasn't been fed yet. Why would I deceive you? There's no reason for me to do that.' (jhovudi1/Reddit)
Box office success

The film's reach extends beyond social media. It took in more than $15 million US during its opening weekend, the second-largest opening weekend for a non-musical documentary in domestic box office history, behind only 2004's Fahrenheit 9/11.

It's also currently the highest-rated movie in Rotten Tomatoes history, currently sitting at 97 per cent fresh. The audience response has also prompted A24 to mount an ambitious Oscars campaign, seeking consideration for You Can See Everything in categories including best picture and best director — an unprecedented push for a feature documentary.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.
With files from Helen Surgenor

articles.title: Seven oil tankers carrying 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel sail towards US
articles.summary:
Tankers, tracked by Greenpeace, are first phase of Trump-Putin deal – but there is uncertainty over whether they will unload

Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor

blocks.text: Seven oil tankers carrying an estimated 288,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are now sailing towards the US, though it is uncertain if the vessels will be able to unload amid a political row about the legality of the shipments.

The transport, tracked by the pressure group Greenpeace, is the first phase of a contentious supply deal negotiated between presidents Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin earlier this month, reversing years of sanctions on Russia oil.

Previous reports had counted three tankers that had departed Russian oil terminals in the Baltic Sea, but using a range of sources, including shipping tracking websites, Greenpeace believes its monitoring exercise is the most complete yet.

Shaun Burnie, an energy specialist with Greenpeace Ukraine, argued that now the location of the tankers could be plotted on a map, the shipments should be halted by Congress or local authorities in the US.
“Instead of rewarding Russia for its vile war against Ukraine, there needs to be more punitive sanctions against Russia,” he said. “These shipments can be stopped”.

One of the seven tankers, Taurus, is relatively close to the US, but at the time the map was first published, five of the others were close to the UK, and three were sailing through or into the English Channel.

In Ukraine, 14 people were reported killed on Thursday morning when a Russian drone struck a crowded train platform in the central city of Dnipro. Five others were reported killed in daytime strikes in two other cities, Chernihiv and Kremenchuk.

Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway company, said a high speed jet-powered drone had struck as a commuter train was preparing to depart Dnipro’s main station. Bodies lay scattered after the relatively unusual daytime attack, which took place at around 11am.

Putin agreed to supply the US with 1.8m tonnes of diesel in a surprise deal announced on 9 October, starting with 300,000 tonnes immediately. Trump announced a six-month waiver on existing sanctions to allow the shipments to proceed.

Russia had been hit by waves of economic sanctions from the US, EU, UK and other leading western economies since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. But this autumn, Trump has altered course and tried to work more closely with Putin, even though Russia has not stopped attacking its neighbour.

blocks.caption: Emergency workers at the scene of a purported Russian drone attack on Dnipro’s main station on Thursday. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Earlier this week, a group of US lawmakers, led by a handful of Democratic senators, warned banks and port authorities that they could face congressional investigations and other legal action if they handled the Russian diesel.

Mikie Sherrill, the Democratic governor of New Jersey, said she was looking at how to prevent the diesel from being unloaded, if an attempt was made to do so in her state. She described the deal as “corrupt and illegal”.

There have been reports that the White House has been trying to encourage US firms to take the oil, though it is not clear buyers are forthcoming, given the legal risks so close to next Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Trump’s popularity has waned as fuel prices in the US have soared since he attacked Iran in the spring. Polling suggests a high likelihood that control of the House of Representatives could pass to the Democrats in the elections, while the battle over the Senate is considered too close to call.

The US president had argued that the Russia deal would help lower diesel prices, though the price per gallon has risen from $6.28 at the time the agreement was announced to $6.33, according to the American Automobile Association.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, denounced the agreement because the money raised would help the Kremlin fund the ongoing war. “Backroom deals” gave Putin more chances on the battlefield, he said.

The Kremlin has been trying to keep information about the latest oil exports secret. A presidential decree from the end of September restricted the publication of information about oil exports in an effort to evade international sanctions.

articles.title: EU seeks 'highest level' ties with Canada in Montreal summit
articles.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said EU seeks "association without accession" for Canada, after EU members snub "associate member" designation.

image.caption: The EU is seeking to build a partnership "closer to membership than anything we have done before," Ursula von der Leyen said.Image: Anne Pollmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: European Union and Canadian leaders met on Thursday during a summit in Montreal, at a special Canada-EU summit to discuss critical policies like artificial inteligence (AI), climate, energy and ⁠security.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU will continue to explore Canada's prospects for becoming the bloc's first "associate member."
But despite her comments, the summit's declaration is expected to exclude the term "associate member," a move pushed by Germany and other members.
"Our idea is simple: it is an association without accession," Von der Leyen clarified. "We can build a partnership that comes closer to membership than anything we have done before."
"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen added.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had said this week he wasn't concerned about the "associate member" status, or "specific names" to be given to the new alliance with the EU.
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney added.
Canada's EU ties are part of a broader strategy, expert tells DW
Ottawa's quest for deeper ties to Europe is seen as a move to reduce its reliance on the US since President Donald Trump imposed tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Frederic Merand, political expert on EU-Canada relations at the University of Montreal, spoke to DW about how the summit serves as "political impetus" to improve the bilateral trade relationship and to free Canada of its reliance on the US.

"It's not going to happen, over time, overnight. And every time we move closer to the Europeans, we realize how dependent we are on the US and how also vulnerable we are to, for example, us retaliation," Merand said.

But he added that courting the EU is also part of a broader strategy "to reinvent the Canadian economy, to create a single market, to attract more investment," as well as to diversify our partnerships with China, India and also other parts of the world.
The EU is "a natural partner" to work with, Merand said, given its existing free trade agreement with Canada, in addition to the close historical and cultural ties between the two partners.
Are the EU and Canada moving closer?
What's on the agenda for the summit?

An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Canada and the EU sought to align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.
Canada has critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines, something for which Europe normally relies on China.
But Canada is in need of major infrastructure investment to develop its mining industry.
There are hopes that the summit can result in a plan for the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
EU and Canadian leaders are also looking into a digital trade deal that can allow for faster and cheaper online transactions.
Additionally, Canada could be allowed to participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad.

articles.title: Dirty tricks or much ado about nothing? Why Alaska, for once, is front and centre in midterms
articles.summary: Could a manoeuvre reportedly plotted by officials connected to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola backfire and cost the party in its attempt to regain control of the Senate in next week's midterms?…

image.caption: This combination photo shows Sen. Dan Sullivan, left, and Dan J. Sullivan, right. Both will appear on the ballot for a Senate seat in Alaska on Tuesday, despite Washington's objections and Republican accusations of political chicanery by the Democrats. (Mark Thiessen, Becky Bohrer/The Associated Pre

blocks.text: The presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the Alaska ballot for a Senate election has attracted attention for about six months now in U.S. political news coverage.

Right-wing media outlets have suspected it was not a mere coincidence, but an example of chicanery, and an investigation by the New York Times resulted in an article Wednesday that suggests a co-ordinated effort by individuals associated with Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign to recruit anyone with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.
A spokesperson for the Peltola campaign had previously said it had "no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."

While political action committees and campaigns for both parties have occasionally engaged in similar "ballot-stacking" tactics that appeared to have the express purpose of siphoning votes from well-established politicians, the Alaska scenario is perhaps the most high-profile example yet seen.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said Wednesday it "should be" illegal, and U.S. President Donald Trump has suggested that criminal prosecutions should result, without specifying on what grounds, or for which particular individuals.
Here's a look at how we got here and the questions that have emerged ahead of Tuesday's midterms.
The facts

Several candidates appeared on the Senate ballot in the spring, including incumbent Dan Sullivan, whose middle name is Scott. But also on the ballot was Republican Dan J. Sullivan. A retired schoolteacher, he is a neophyte in terms of political office and has registered as a Democrat in the past.

In June, the state's Republican lieutenant-governor disqualified Dan J. Sullivan under a state regulation that forbids ballot names that are "confusing or misleading to voters or compromises the fairness or neutrality of the ballot."

A campaign spokesperson for Democratic Senate hopeful Mary Peltola, seen in Anchorage, Alaska, on Oct. 14, has previously said it had 'no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.' (Becky Bohrer/The Associated Press)

But a state judge's reversal of that decision was upheld by the Alaska Supreme Court. The gist of their ruling was that there is no statutory or constitutional mechanism to remove a person from the ballot if they had met the qualifications to register as a candidate, no matter the origin story of the candidacy.

"There's a lot of different ways you can distinguish these two candidates on the ballot, short of precluding access to the ballot to begin with," Aimee Oravec, an Alaska justice, said during oral arguments in the case.
Why it matters

What the composition of the Senate will look like after its three-dozen races are called is seen as an unpredictable puzzle by pollsters. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority ⁠and Democrats need four pickups to regain control of the chamber, so the race between Peltola and the incumbent Sullivan could be pivotal.
Alaska is one of the smallest electorates. Sullivan was elected to office in 2014 by two percentage points, which translated to just over 6,000 more votes than his opponent.

In the all-party primary in August to determine the top four candidates, the candidate derisively nicknamed "Decoy Dan" by some garnered 4,107 votes, about 2 per cent of the total vote. This despite the fact he's reportedly spent no money on campaign staff or media.

Democrats have defended the manoeuvre as an example of political hardball. They have pointed to examples nationally of Republican-led efforts to place candidates on ballots as a diversionary tactic, and Alaska Democrats alleged in 2024 that Republicans were behind a scheme to get an incarcerated candidate — who's running again this year — on the ballot to siphon votes from their preferred U.S. House candidate.

Peltola and her campaign haven't fully addressed the Times allegations, merely calling it a "diversion." The revelation could backfire for Peltola, a Yup'ik who became the first Indigenous person from Alaska to ever serve in Congress when she won a House seat in 2022.
In addition to Sullivan, Republican Lisa Murkowski, the other U.S. senator from Alaska, is calling for her to come clean about her knowledge of the scheme.

items: U.S. midterms could be the country's most expensive elections yet. To what end?
Why the Hispanic vote could sway the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections

blocks.text: The gambit could also just breed more general cynicism in a country where unfounded allegations of vote fraud in the 2020 election led to a riot at the U.S. Capitol.
"How does this increase voter confidence in our election process?" the Juneau Empire, the newspaper out of the state capital, asked in a recent editorial.
Legal fallout
After the Times article landed, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said he was directing the state's Department of Public Safety to investigate the scheme to see if criminal or civil offences occurred.
"Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections," said Dunleavy.
Trump accused of mounting fear-based intimidation campaign ahead of U.S. midterms
Several days before the Times exposé landed, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit to demand that Alaska be blocked from certifying a Peltola win if Dan J. Sullivan remains on the ballot.

Trump said he had ordered the department to do that and no criticism emerged in Congress from Republicans who regularly lobbed accusations about a politicized Justice Department under Democratic predecessor Joe Biden.
Legal questions
It is hard to predict if any criminality occurred, given what is known so far. But vote-siphoning schemes have led to charges for individuals before.

As for the Justice Department suit, the U.S. Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Election experts are pessimistic about its chances for success, and even the Trump-friendly Wall Street Journal editorial page called it a "legal Hail Mary."

"The statute simply doesn't let the Department of Justice enjoin certification," Derek Muller, University of Notre Dame law professor, told the Associated Press last week. "The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month."

The lawsuit asks the court to block certification until an investigation determines whether enough voters were fooled in a way that swings the election. It doesn't explain how that would happen, and the right to privacy provides another complication, as votes are supposed to be confidential.

Election expert Rick Hasen called the Times report a "bombshell" and said perjury prosecutions were possible if it could be established someone lied about involvement in the scheme. But Hasen, UCLA law professor and director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project, wrote Wednesday on his blog that he didn't think the new reporting changed the equation on the Justice Department suit.
Hasen also said he didn't see any mechanism for the government to criminalize Dan J. Sullivan's campaign.

"And if it could do so, then it could be a crime every time that the Republican Party backs a Green Party candidate, or Democrats support a MAGA candidate in a primary in the hopes that the candidate would be weaker against a Democrat in the general election," he said.
The ballot wrinkle
A sample election ballot for Alaska shows how the two Sullivan's running for a Senate seat are being distinguished. (Haven Daley/The Associated Press)
Alaska employs a ranked-choice ballot. Some local editorials, as well as the Wall Street Journal, have argued that such a system encourages the possibility of voter confusion and sham candidates.

Democrats counter that the local electorate has likely been inundated for months with stories and video differentiating the two men. In addition, they say, a voter could just simply choose not to rank Peltola at all on their ballot, with the likelihood that the less seasoned Sullivan comes out on top over the man who's represented Alaska for over a decade considered remote.

items: US Politics! Will Texas flip, who's bailing on Trump?
Democrats promise Epstein probes will be a priority if they win midterms, but to what end?

blocks.text: It's not the citizenry's first go-round with the system, which has been in place since 2022. Even Republican Murkowski, criticizing the Justice Department suit last week, has said that "Alaskans don't need any help voting for their preferred candidates."
It is too late to change ballots. Dan J. Sullivan is listed as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.," without a party label, and Dan S. Sullivan is listed as "Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent."

articles.title: Hong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 people
articles.summary:
Blaze last year was deadliest housing fire globally since 1980 and some ex-residents and victims’ families say they still need justice

Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for government…

blocks.text: Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families.
The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies.
Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned.

Last November, a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an inferno that enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations.

Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980.
Authorities have filed charges, including manslaughter, against seven individuals and two companies over their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested.
The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”.

Had the four departments better recognised the risks and acted accordingly, “there was a real possibility that the misconduct of the private-sector parties and the fire hazards in WF Court could have been rectified or removed before the fire”, it said.
Lee said a three-month investigation would now begin into the government’s role.
“I am deeply saddened. I would like to apologise to the affected residents and the general public,” Lee said on Thursday, adding that housing minister Ho should “bear political responsibility”.

But Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife and home in the fire, told reporters he did not consider the government’s acceptance of accountability adequate. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said, according to AFP news agency. “Administrative responsibility falls short” and political accountability even more so, Yip added.
Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the fire, told AP news agency that progress had been made but that justice had yet to be served.
She added the officials’ apology was late, though it was better than nothing.
Hong Kong’s government has previously been accused by critics of being more concerned with clamping down on criticism rather than addressing the causes of the disaster.
Since a National Security Law was imposed on the city in 2020 by Beijing, the city’s once vibrant civil society groups and political opposition have been all but quashed.
In the weeks after the fire, authorities warned against crimes that “exploit the tragedy” and reportedly arrested at least three people for sedition.
China’s national security agency in Hong Kong also summoned international media representatives, saying they had smeared the government in their reports on the fire.
On Thursday Lee promised that ““similar incidents will never be allowed to happen again”.
Some observers had called for a more legally powerful inquiry commission to be set up, rather than the judge-led independent review committee that compiled Thursday’s report.
Lee told reporters that authorities had proposed “systematic reforms”, including criminalising bid-rigging and overhauling the complaints system.
The report stated: “The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun.”

articles.title: Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor Maya Gebala being released from hospital, father says
articles.summary: A 13-year-old girl who was severely injured in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting is being released from hospital after nearly nine months of uncertain recovery, her father says.

image.caption: David Gebala posted a video of his daughter Maya Gebala to social media on Thursday saying she is being released from hospital nearly nine months after the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting. (David Gebala/Facebook)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New
A 13-year-old girl who was severely injured in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting is being released from hospital after nearly nine months of uncertain recovery, her father says.
The 13-year-old required surgery after she suffered severe injuries in the February mass shooting
David Gebala shared a Facebook video Thursday of his daughter Maya Gebala in a wheelchair reacting with excitement as he tells her she'll be going home.

"It's been 262 days since you were airlifted to B.C. Children's Hospital," he wrote in the post. "262 days since we were told, 'We did everything we could, but we don’t think she’s going to make it through the night.'
"Since then, I’ve watched you fight for every single one of those days."

items: More stories from Northern B.C.

blocks.text: While the family has not been speaking to media, they have been sharing updates through social media posts and videos intended for the public.

In previous posts, Gebala's mother has indicated the family will likely have to permanently relocate to Vancouver in order for Gebala to continue receiving care, though it's not clear whether that is still the case.
Details of her injuries have been shared online and in lawsuits filed in California against tech firm OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman over their alleged roles in the deadly February mass shooting.
Gebala's reaction after her father tells her she'll be leaving hospital. (David Gebala/Facebook)
Documents filed by her family in court in April 2026 say Gebala was shot three times and that a bullet struck her skull and "shattered bone fragments through her brain."
OpenAI has asked for the case to be dismissed.

items: Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor Maya Gebala celebrates 13th birthday as recovery continues
Tumbler Ridge shooting survivor's 5th surgery 'a success,' father says

blocks.text: In May, Gebala's family said she had undergone surgery for a cranioplasty, which involved installing a prosthetic barrier to quell swelling and deflation in Gebala's head that was a symptom of her damaged skull.

It was the fifth surgery Gebala had gone through since the shooting, and in the time since, the family has shared video of her on various outings throughout Vancouver, as she is no longer confined to B.C. Children's Hospital where she has been receiving her treatment.
Those include celebrations from her 13th birthday in September when she attended a Foo Fighters concert at B.C. Place, and enjoyed cake and games.

articles.title: More prisoners recalled to jail than released in England and Wales
articles.summary:
Ministry of Justice figures show recalls rose 27% in year to June despite emergency measures to ease overcrowding

More people were recalled to jails in England and Wales in the first half of…

blocks.text: More people were recalled to jails in England and Wales in the first half of this year than were released, despite government efforts to reduce the prison population, according to figures released on Thursday.

Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data shows that 12,338 people were recalled to custody between the beginning of April and the end of June, while 12,278 people were released. It continues a trend set between January and March, when 13,193 people were returned to prison and 12,977 released.
A total of 52,716 prisoners were put back behind bars in the year to June after breaching the terms of their licence – 27% up on the previous 12-month total.
The high recall rate is a key contributor to the prison capacity crisis and helped to prompt early release schemes earlier this month.

The MoJ figures also show 79,274 inmates were freed early from prison between September 2024 and June 2026 under emergency measures brought in by the government to try to tackle the overcrowding crisis.

The move, known as the SDS40 early release scheme, cut the proportion of sentences some prisoners must serve in England and Wales from 50% to 40%. It is one of several policy changes that are likely to have contributed to the rise in recalls, the MoJ said.
The emergency measures were replaced with a permanent scheme for early releases from 1 October under the Sentencing Act 2026.

The Howard League for Penal Reform said the “alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse”, as it called on the government to find a “lasting solution” to the overcrowding crisis.

Rob Preece, the head of communications at the Howard League, said: “The prison system is under enormous pressure, with chronic overcrowding, staff shortages and awful conditions that make it close to impossible to rehabilitate people effectively. Imposing ever longer sentences has led us to this crisis, but the alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse.”

The MoJ said it was “vital those who break the rules can be hauled back to prison”. The department said the rise in recalls amid SDS40 releases was also likely to have been influenced by policy changes that result in most offenders being taken back into custody for 56 days before being released again – known as a fixed-term recall – instead of being held until the end of their sentence.

Incidents of self-harm and violence have remained high as pressure on the prison system has grown. Safety in custody statistics showed that 360 people in prison died in the 12 months to the end of September 2026, including 66 people who died in circumstances recorded as “self-inflicted”.

Prisons recorded 68,231 incidents of self-harm in the 12 months to the end of June 2026, at a rate of one every eight minutes. Self-harm incidents fell by 12% in men’s prisons and fell by 3.8% in women’s prisons.
A separate dataset showed that the number of serious offenders on probation who were charged with a serious further offence had increased for the third successive year, to a record number.

Of 281 serious offenders charged, 119 were registered sexual offenders, 128 were murderers, and four were terrorists or posed a terror risk, according to figures on multi-agency public protection arrangements.

articles.title: Spain begins mourning period as search continues for train crash victims
articles.summary: Emergency services, drones and dog unit continue to comb carriages as Civil Guard sets up clinics for relatives to provide DNA samples
articles.byline: Sam Jones and Ashifa Kassam in Madrid

blocks.text: Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.

The trains – one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo – were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
Spain’s foreign ministry said 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, adding that one had been killed and at least seven injured.

blocks.caption: Iryo employees in Madrid embrace after observing a minute’s silence for the victims of the train crash. Photograph: Bernat Armangué/AP

blocks.text: The crash came 10 months after 46 people were killed and dozens more injured when two trains – one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

The disaster has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain’s large, modern high-speed rail network. The transport minister, Óscar Puente, said rear-end collisions such as Wednesday’s were “highly unlikely”, and suggested the accident could have been caused by human error under “inexplicable” circumstances.

blocks.caption: The crash scene on Wednesday. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Emergency services combed the wreckage through the night for more victims, using cranes to hoist pieces of mangled metal. At daybreak, police once again launched drones to survey the crash site.

Emiliano García-Page, the leader of the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on Thursday morning that rescue teams did not think they would find any more bodies in one damaged carriage that was ‌still overturned, but added that body parts had been found that would need to be identified.

“Yesterday we experienced a catastrophe that without a doubt has left all of Spain in shock,” said García-Page. He confirmed that 50 of the people who had been taken to hospitals in the region were still being treated.

The prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, speaking during a visit to the emergency command centre in the city of Toledo, said the authorities were doing all they could to establish the cause of the crash and prevent another rail tragedy.

blocks.caption: World Central Kitchen delivers meals to emergency services and security forces at the scene of the train collision. Photograph: Angeles Visdomine/EPA

blocks.text: “I’d like to let all Spaniards know that every institution that is part of the state – from the smallest municipality to the government of Spain – is working day and night, not only to provide a response to the families of the victims, but also, of course, to uncover every last detail of this tragedy and to strengthen safety measures so that something like this never happens again.”
King Felipe, who visited a hospital in Toledo where some of the injured were being treated, said Spain had “once again suffered an extremely harsh blow” and called for lessons to be learned.

“There is obviously an ongoing investigation, which should establish how and why this tragedy happened,” he said on Thursday. “Measures will need to be looked at and adopted so that this doesn’t happen again.”

Meanwhile, Spanish train drivers went ahead with a previously planned strike to press for more investment in railway safety. The crash was Europe’s deadliest train accident since a derailment in Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain that killed 80 people in 2013.

“We will continue demanding the necessary measures to make this sector safe again ... It must have all the safety systems required to maintain the quality standards we have always had,” said Diego Martín of the train drivers’ union Semaf. “We cannot tolerate, under any circumstances, this type of incident happening again.”

The Guardia Civil police force has set up four offices in the cities of Madrid, Toledo, Córdoba and Seville to enable relatives to provide DNA samples and help identify victims. Blood donation points have also been set up in Castilla-La Mancha and Madrid. The force said 64 people had been reported missing by relatives by Thursday morning.

A school in Urda, which lies about 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid, has been turned into an information centre where relatives can inquire about loved ones. Teams of Red Cross workers offered support to groups of people who had arrived, some of them in tears.

Carmen García, a Red Cross psychologist, said “long and hard hours” lay ahead and that “every person will manage it in their own way”. She added: “We have people who are in shock, who haven’t taken on board what has happened, angry people, sad, worried people. The grieving will be complicated.”
José Miguel Fernández, a parish priest in Urda, joined the emergency services in offering support to the victims’ families.

“It is important for relatives to find their loved ones, even if they have died, because the grieving process is quicker when you have been able to say goodbye at that final moment,” he told Onda Cero radio.
Survivors have spoken of being thrown from their seats by the impact of the crash, and of trying to help the injured in the immediate aftermath.

Among the first victims to be named was José Manuel Chacón, a 31-year-old Guardia Civil officer. The national law enforcement agency expressed its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends and colleagues.

Also among those killed was Fátima Báñez, a former labour minister for the conservative People’s party (PP), who had gone on to chair the social and corporate responsibility arm of Spain’s ⁠employers’ association.

The PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, called for an immediate investigation into what had happened, as well as a “complete and independent review” of Spain’s entire rail network. “Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure,” he told reporters.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Female Lib Dem MP accuses Nigel Farage of shoving her in parliament
articles.summary:
Caroline Voaden says the Reform UK leader grabbed her by the arm and tried to push past her in incident in May

•

blocks.text: A female Liberal Democrat MP has accused Nigel Farage of shoving her aside at the state opening of parliament after which one of her male colleagues intervened.

Caroline Voaden gave her account of the incident in May this year after Farage revealed on Wednesday that there had been a “physical altercation” in parliament which meant he had decided to avoid the budget.

Voaden told the Guardian: “He was trying to get out of the chamber and instead of just asking if he could go past, he said: ‘Let me past’. I turned round and said: ‘No, you can wait your turn like everyone else’. He grabbed me by the arm or the shoulder, pushed me to one side and tried to push past me. One of my colleagues tried to stop him because he thought I was going to fall down the stairs. And then we all shuffled down.

“Quite deliberately, he grabbed me by the arm from behind and pushed me to one side so that I fell into a colleague or the wall on the other side. I was really taken aback and really angry because I think you just don’t behave like that in any workplace, let alone the chamber of the House of Commons. It was rude. It was nasty.”
Voaden said she had complained to the sergeant at arms who she believed had written to Farage asking him to apologise. She also raised it with the speaker. “Nothing ever came of it,” she said.

blocks.caption: Caroline Voaden speaking in parliament. Photograph: House of Commons

blocks.text: A Reform UK source said it was “not true at all, it was the Lib Dem MPs being aggressive towards Nigel. This is typical Lib Dem dishonesty in an attempt to stay relevant.”
The male Lib Dem MP who intervened is understood to be Max Wilkinson, with sources saying he put a hand on Farage’s shoulder, “fairly gently” grabbed him and said he could not do that to another MP.
Reform sources also suggested a video from the Commons showed her account was wrong, but the Lib Dems said the incident took place before the footage started.

The row erupted after the Reform leader said he had skipped John Healey’s budget speech in the Commons on Wednesday because his seat reservation had been moved and he decided to give it a “wide berth” in order to “avoid conflict” in the chamber.
He claimed he had been involved in a “physical altercation” with another MP on the day of the state opening of parliament in May.
It later emerged his reservation had been removed by Commons staff as it did not have the proper date stamp.
Daisy Cooper, the Lib Dem deputy leader, told Sky News on Thursday morning that her party’s MPs were involved in the May incident mentioned by Farage.

She said: “My understanding – I didn’t see it, I wasn’t there – but my understanding is that he physically shoved one of our female MPs out of the way, and that one of our male MPs then challenged him on that.
“I didn’t see it, I didn’t witness what happened, but that was several months ago.
“And let’s be really clear: it’s Reform UK that had a problem at their conference with bundling female journalists and members out of their hall. So, we’ll take no lessons from them on this.”
Afterwards, Voaden posted on social media in response to Farage’s claim that he was at risk of “another physical altercation”: “We both know that’s not true Nigel don’t we?
“I’m still waiting for the apology you were required to write to me … Though I won’t hold my breath.”
When asked for a response to the accusations, Robert Jenrick, Reform’s shadow chancellor, said: “You know what? I am sick to death of these pathetic Westminster debates.
“The thing about Reform politicians is, yeah, we love parliament, the institution of parliament. I go there every day. I speak in parliament. I represent my constituents.

“But I’m much more interested about, actually, the issues, trying to change this country, getting out and about outside of the bubble. And I’m not interested in even responding, dignifying the nonsense that Daisy Cooper is talking about there.”

articles.title: Cuts like a knife: Canadian rocker Bryan Adams trolls Trump with new song
articles.summary:
Rocker wrote a ‘love letter’ to Canada with a new album – and some pointed commentary about the US president

Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has…

blocks.text: Lake Ontario, the vast body of water that straddles the US-Canada border, has gone by many names over the centuries: Lac Saint-Louis, Lacus Ontarius, Skaniadorio, Cataraqui Lake. But one thing it will never be called, says Canadian rock star Bryan Adams, is Lake America.
In his new song Lake Ontario, Adams takes aim at the US president, Donald Trump, accusing him of “breaking the peace” between the people who live on the lake’s shores.

Trump signed an executive order in August directing US federal agencies to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America”, echoing his earlier, widely mocked decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico “the Gulf of America”.

The move further escalated a feud with Canada that has strained the longstanding alliance between the two countries. Trump’s decision has largely been met with derision in Canada, with some pointing out that the province of Ontario is named after the lake, not the other way around. Adams’ lyrics emphasise the roots of the name:
double quotation markThe ‘lake of shining waters’ is what the Iroquois called her It’s a First Nations name – not an executive order.

Adams’s lyrics also suggest that Trump’s naming stunt was intended to deflect from the president’s other political problems, including the war in Iran and renewed scrutiny of the Jeffrey Epstein files.
double quotation markBut things weren’t going his way in Iran So like a baby tossing the toys from the pram But it feels like another distraction While the Epstein files were getting traction

The song is part of what Adams described in a recent interview as a broader “love letter” to Canada: a songwriting project that began with an invitation from a film company to write about the Maritimes provinces of Canada and has since morphed into the upcoming album How’s It Goin’.
“After finishing the first song, I moved on to that one, and then moved on to another one, and then started thinking maybe I should just carry on with my theme,” he said.
As well as homages to Canadian heroes, the album also includes 51st State, released on 1 July – Canada Day – as another repudiation of Trump, in this case his efforts to annex Canada.
after newsletter promotion
double quotation markYou can push us to the brink But where the open road divides You’ll find a wall of maple With us on the other side.
The first time he played the song in public was in the US.
“We weren’t sure how people were going to respond to it,” he said. “But we got a standing ovation every night for it. It made me think: perhaps, finally, the tide’s turning.”

articles.title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win
articles.summary:
The trouncing of the far right provides a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France

Thank you, Brazil,…

blocks.text: Thank you, Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France.

The astonishing comeback victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.

Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced a record fall in Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zero deforestation by 2030 and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south.

Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.

In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return.

blocks.caption: Indigenous activists protesting at last year’s Cop30 summit in Brazil. Photograph: André Penner/AP

blocks.text: So although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways:

1 Politics matter. There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the 59.5% surge of Amazon deforestation under the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements.

2 Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities. In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses.

blocks.caption: Pro-Lula supporters rally in Copacabana after Lula’s first-round defeat. Photograph: Bob Karp/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: 3 Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp.

4 Go on the offensive against US tech giants. Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools. Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats in Colombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.”

blocks.caption: A Lula supporter holds up a mask of Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg at a protest over alleged electoral interference outside the firm’s São Paulo headquarters. Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: 5 Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”. Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended.

blocks.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro arriving in Florida after losing to Lula. Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images

blocks.text: 6 Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violent gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrations of 2018.

7 Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability. Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US). They highlighted the interlinked threats posed by the obsequience to Trump, Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and his promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of the planetary boundaries essential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.

The former environment minister Marina Silva pulled these threads together during the victory celebrations, saying Brazil had come together against these threats: “Long live the people who emerged from every corner of Brazil to sow hope for a future that is socially just, sovereign, democratic and sustainable.”
Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action. Now it needs others to follow.

articles.title: Metropolitan police refers itself to watchdog over Meghan warning letter
articles.summary:
Announcement made as Philippines police investigate suspected child sex abuse images reportedly found at her father’s former home


The Metropolitan police says it has…

blocks.text: The Metropolitan police says it has voluntarily referred itself to the official watchdog for failing to pass on a letter detailing allegations against the Duchess of Sussex’s father.
The announcement comes as police in the Philippines investigate suspected child sexual abuse images reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former home.

Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told the Sun last week that he found a stash of child sex abuse images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines and reported it to local police and the FBI.
Markle Sr has admitted paying for sex in the south-east Asian country but denies possessing illicit material.
The Met said it received a letter in 2019 in which the author suggested “they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex”.

The Met said although the letter “did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom”.
It was passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, the force said.

It added that – after a review – a voluntary referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct “in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex”.

Commander Adam Slonecki, who leads the Met’s protection command, said: “In January 2019, the Met received a letter addressed to our protection command, specifically the fixated threats assessment centre.

“The author of the letter suggested they were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.
“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness.

“The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies. In recent days, the Met’s directorate of professional standards has carried out an initial review into our actions following receipt of the letter in 2019.

“Following that review, a voluntary referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies, and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

“In addition, it is our intention to make a number of referrals to relevant overseas law enforcement agencies in relation to the allegations contained within the letter. That process is under way and will be completed in the coming days.”

articles.title: Israel election: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud claims large-scale foreign involvement in the elections led by Qatar and Turkey, with Israel’s authorities so far refuting the claims.

image.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud believes voter fraud took place in IsraelImage: Ronen Zvulun/REUTERS

blocks.text: Israel woke up on Thursday to allegations by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party that foreign actors may have sought to influence voter mobilization efforts in Arab communities during this week's legislative election.
No'am Sohlberg, the Supreme Court judge who heads Israel's Central Election Committee, sent a letter to Israel's internal security agency Shin Bet to look into the Likud's claims.

According to Likud's statement, Arab parties Ra'am and the Joint List — which received a record share of the vote, mostly due to unprecedented turnout in communities of Arab and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship — allegedly used "severe criminal offenses" to spur voters to go to the polls, including bribery, threats and other forms of election fraud.

"Severe suspicions were brought to my attention about improper intervention in the elections by foreign funding by outside actors that act against the Israeli interest," Sohlberg wrote in the letter, adding that he was "unable to testify" as to whether the allegations are true.

blocks.caption: The Likud party has complained about alleged voter fraud in Arab communitiesImage: Katrine Dige Houmoller/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party claimed in a statement. His own coalition lost seats, leaving both the prime minister and his opponents short of a majority — unless they were to work with one or both of the Arab parties.

Likud and other right-wing figures pointed to the unusually high turnout in Arab communities, reports of organized transportation to polling stations and concerns over foreign-funded voter mobilization campaigns as grounds for requesting an investigation. They argue that a formal review is necessary to maintain public confidence in the electoral process, regardless of whether wrongdoing is ultimately found.
Authorities refute allegations

Israel's elections are administered by the Central Election Committee, a body comprising representatives of parliamentary parties and chaired by a Supreme Court justice. Large-scale election fraud has historically been rare, although disputes over campaign conduct and voting procedures regularly arise.
Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”

blocks.caption: Left-wing demonstrators demanded that the Arab parties be allowed to take part in Israel's new governmentImage: Ilia Yefimovich/AFP

blocks.text: "Election day went with a minority of irregular incidents in the area of election integrity, also compared to other elections," it said in a statement.
A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.

"We don't have any basis for claims of 'stolen elections,'" Dean Livne, the Committee's acting director general, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan 11, adding that the committee received "claims rather than evidence" from Likud and other parties.

Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor and the head of the Yashar party, blamed the Israeli leader for leading an "improper influence operation" to cast doubt on the elections and create what he called "a fictive delegitimization" for the next parliament.
However, Eisenkot, also called for Likud's allegation of electoral fraud to be investigated.
The religious Muslim Ra'am party denied any involvement and said it would cooperate with any investigation.
Qatar released a statement denying any involvement in the Israeli elections, calling them "false propaganda aimed at dragging Qatar's name into Israel's political conflicts."
The controversy comes against the backdrop of growing polarization in Israeli politics and increasing public distrust between rival political camps.

Likud's motivation could be to decrease the Arab influence on Israeli politics, according to Amira Halperin, a senior fellow at the Palm Beach Center for Democracy and Policy Research. "The Arab votes were very, very important in this election," she said.

blocks.caption: The Arab parties celebrated their historic success in Israel's electionImage: Jamal Awad/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Such allegations could also hurt the public's trust in the election process Halperin argued: "We need to be cautious about predicting a failure of the democratic system."
Shin Bet head in focus

Israeli media reports have suggested that some of the concerns cited by Likud were based on intelligence assessments examined by the Shin Bet, though the agency has not publicly confirmed the details of any such findings.

Public broadcaster Kan reported the suspicions' extent as "relatively small," citing sources familiar with the Shin Bet investigation. Israeli daily Ha'aretz, too, quoted sources familiar with the allegations as saying the reports are "being blown out of proportion.”

David Zini, the head of the agency, said on election day that the elections in Israel are "safe, sound and supervised," adding that the Elections Committee and Israeli police are "successfully" preventing anyone from hurting it.

Zini's appointment earlier this year was criticized by opposition figures, who questioned both his qualifications for the role and Netanyahu's motives in selecting him. Supporters of the appointment rejected those criticisms, arguing that Zini's military experience and security background made him suitable for the position.

Separately, the Shin Bet, has been involved in investigating several of Netanyahu's closest aides on allegations of undisclosed ties to Qatar. Those investigations are unrelated to the current election allegations.
Pre-planned tactics?

Israeli outlet N12 has reported that in the weekend before the elections that Likud officials were discussing potential election-integrity complaints ahead of voting, although no evidence of actual irregularities had been presented at that stage, with a focus on Arab and Palestinian communities .
"They sat and brainstormed to find creative ideas of how to complain about this issue," said Daphna Liel, the reporter who broke the story.

blocks.caption: Voter turnout reached historic levels during Israel's electionImage: Jalaa Marey/AFP

blocks.text: Historic turnout
Arab and Palestinian participation in this week's election was unprecedented, with turnout jumping from around 50% in 2022 to about 80% in 2026, according to reports in Israel.

Arab voter participation has fluctuated significantly in recent decades. Turnout has often been influenced by debates within Arab society over whether participation in national elections can effectively advance the interests of Arab citizens, who comprise roughly 20% of Israel's population. The exceptionally high turnout in this election was widely seen as a sign of renewed political mobilization.

blocks.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party campaigned with the slogan "right wing or Palestine"Image: Jewel Samad/AFP

blocks.text: This resulted in huge success forthe Joint List and Ra'am, with 11 and eight parliament seats, respectively, in comparison to six and four in the 2022 election. Both parties have already voiced their willingness to cooperate with Israel's Zionist opposition to replace Netanyahu.
Most parties in Israel's Zionist opposition promised not to join a coalition with Arab parties ahead of the elections, with the exception of left-wing Zionist party "The Democrats” (HaDemocratim).

On election day, there were also allegations over "systematic delays" in voting in Arab and Palestinian polling stations, according to Adalah, an Israeli-Palestinian NGO for the legal rights of the Arab minority in Israel.
No clear winner emerges in Israel's election

articles.title: Israeli leader Netanyahu accused of using ‘ugly’ smear tactics to cling to power
articles.summary:
Prime minister claims Arab Israeli parties used foreign backing to steal elections, in which his coalition lost its majority

•

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.

Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel, supposedly funded by foreign money.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.
“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.

The prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.

On Wednesday night, the prime minister posted a statement by Likud online, which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.

Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, holding the balance of power.

The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.

The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”
Opposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.

Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.

Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.

The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.
The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.

It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.

With almost all the votes counted, Netanyahu’s coalition has 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s bloc has 48, and the Joint List and Ra’am together have 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.

The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.
On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.

Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.

Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.

The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.

One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.
Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.

“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.

Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are being accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.
“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.

articles.title: Canada to invest up to $1.6B in Toronto-based AI company Cohere
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney announces an investment in Canadian AI company Cohere, in Montreal on Thursday. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·New
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian AI company Cohere.
PM Carney says Canada won't wait for AI to be decided by other countries Canada doesn't trust
The Canadian government is taking an equity stake in Cohere, joining a funding round led by Germany's Schwarz Group targeting ‌$7 billion for the Toronto-based AI lab, Cohere said on Thursday.

The round would value Cohere at about $36 billion. Schwarz, which owns the Lidl and Kaufland retail ​chains, pledged $780 million to lead the round in ​April as part of Cohere's merger with the German AI developer Aleph Alpha.
Cohere said the money will fund ​model development, products for regulated industries and computing infrastructure.
Prime Minister Mark Carney made the announcement Thursday as he welcomed European Union leaders to Montreal for a summit aimed at forging closer ties.
He said ‌Ottawa would invest up to $1.6 billion in Cohere. Other investors included Nvidia and BCE's Bell Canada subsidiary, he said.
"Cohere will stay Canadian, creating more opportunities for our workers and businesses. ⁠Its incorporation and headquarters will remain here," he said in a speech.
Company to invest $1.7B in new infrastructure by 2030
Carney said Canada won't wait for the future of artificial intelligence to be decided elsewhere by those Canadians don't know or trust.
Cohere will invest at least $1.7 billion in new computing infrastructure in Canada ‌by 2030, he added.
Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez called the government's investment "a huge honour."
Why slowing the AI race won't be easy

Schwarz, which owned more than 20 per cent of Aleph Alpha, spent almost $25 billion on new data centres in Germany. Schwarz ​Digits CEO Christian Müller said the group plans to run Cohere's models on its STACKIT ⁠cloud, calling the investment the next step after the Aleph Alpha ⁠deal.
Cohere has completed only an initial close of the round ⁠and did ⁠not say how much ​has been committed so far or when it expects the round to ​close.
The company said ⁠annual recurring revenue grew 165 per cent year over year as of the third quarter and that its customer count has grown to 300.
With files from The Canadian Press
