articles.title: Ship reported on fire off Oman as Iran escalation fears mount
articles.summary: A ship in the Strait of Hormuz is reported to be on fire, a British maritime agency says. Iran has meanwhile said it has shot down another US drone as military tensions with Washington continue.

image.caption: Another ship is reportedly on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, seen here from OmanImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: A ship on fire has been reported in the Strait of Hormuz, British maritime agency UKMTO said on Thursday.
The agency, which is run by the British Royal Navy, did not give details on the cause of the blaze or any casualties.
Iran has, however, recently stepped up its attacks on ships that it sees as using the waterway without proper authorization.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that three tankers had exploded and caught fire in the past 24 hours after hitting sea mines while using an "unauthorized" route, but it is not known if the case reported to the UKMTO is one of them.
This comes as Iran has reported shooting down another US drone east of the waterway as fears grow of a new escalation in the US-Iran war.
Iran steps up attacks in Strait of Hormuz
The UKMTO said the captain of another ship had reported the blaze onboard a vessel spotted 9 nautical miles (17 kilometers) north of the town of Khasab in Oman, which is located just off the strait.
The status of ⁠the ​crew is ​unknown, and so far ​no information has emerged pertaining to ⁠damage or environmental ⁠impact.

Since the Middle East war was triggered in February by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Tehran has sought to control the strait, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, and has attacked ships it considers to be unauthorized users of the waterway.
Oil exports through the waterway fell again last week, according to shipping data provider Kpler.
Attacks on ships in the strait are at the highest level since the war began, according to US-based think tank Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait in the area where the burning ship was reportedly sighted.

blocks.caption: The Strait of Hormuz is a vital chokepoint for oil and gas transportImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: US drone downed
The reported ship fire comes as Iran says its forces have downed a drone near the strait, with the Tasnim news agency citing the IRGC as saying a new, advanced air defense system was used.
The report said that Iran's armed forces have destroyed 14 drones of this type and more than 50 MQ-9 Reaper drones since the war broke out.
The claims have not been independently verified, though the US Congressional Research Service says dozens of US aircraft and drones have been reported lost or damaged since the war began.

blocks.caption: The MQ-1 Predator can be used both for surveillance and attackImage: Col. Leslie Pratt/epa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fears of new US strikes
The latest incidents come as US President Donald Trump is widely seen to be considering fresh strikes against Iran after the US midterm elections on November 3.
Last week, Trump said, "we may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli attacks on Tehran in February that triggered the war. He did not, however, give any timeframe.
A third US aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are currently heading to the region.
As reports of a possible renewed escalation swirl, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has reportedly nonetheless fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia.

If confirmed, the ouster would be the latest in a series of such high-level departures under the Trump administration, with Sylvia's predecessor, Lieutenant General Joseph McGee being forced to retire last October.
According to a report in The Atlantic, no reason was given for Sylvia's departure and no replacement has been named.
Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent?

articles.title: [READOUT] How can businesses win back customers amid a weak peso and high inflation?
articles.summary: Businesses must balance rising costs against the dwindling purchasing power and growing frustration of cash-strapped consumers

blocks.text: What can businesses do to win over customers already struggling with high prices? An October study by Organic Intelligence suggests a concrete response some brands could consider.

Asked what would make a brand feel genuinely on their side, the top response was a price freeze (27%), ahead of smaller tingi sizes (16%), free shipping (14%), and promotional bundles (12%). The study’s researchers later told Rappler that a price freeze campaign would be highly effective in building customer loyalty with value-conscious customers.

The findings reflect how financially stretched consumers have become. The survey of 800 urban Filipinos, conducted in May, also found that 42% had borrowed for essentials such as food and transportation, while 45% said inflation had drained their motivation to get ahead.
And the pressure is unlikely to ease in the near-term. September inflation reached 7.2%, with further acceleration expected when October figures come out on November 5.
Meanwhile, businesses must weigh consumer sentiment against how much of their rising costs they can realistically pass on to consumers.

The peso closed at another historic low of P64.17 to the dollar on Tuesday, October 27, despite the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) delivering a larger-than-expected 50 basis point rate hike just five days earlier. That brought its policy rate to 5.50%, following four consecutive increases this year.

After the same Monetary Board meeting, the BSP raised its 2027 inflation forecast from 5.4% to 6%, signaling that businesses may have to contend with higher costs and weaker consumer purchasing power for longer.

The BSP, however, is in no hurry to defend the peso at any particular exchange rate. Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said the central bank would largely let the currency find its own level, intervening only to cushion excessive movements that could worsen inflation.

Former BSP deputy governor Diwa Guinigundo pointed to deeper problems behind the peso’s slide, including weak capital flows, the country’s balance of payments deficit, low foreign investment, and investor uncertainty surrounding corruption allegations and the ongoing messy impeachment trial.
Consider the numbers:

items: The Philippines recorded a $9.1-billion balance of payments deficit in the first nine months of 2026, compared with $5.3 billion a year earlier. Foreign portfolio investments registered $4.25 billion in net outflows from January to August, reversing $4.58 billion in inflows a year earlier.

The country’s hefty import bill also creates enormous demand for dollars. Consider that imports of mineral fuels and related products alone increased by $2.56 billion year on year in the first half of 2026.
And the pressure could persist. The BSP forecasts another $8.5-billion balance of payments deficit in 2027, alongside a $19.4-billion current account deficit.

Foreign exchange reserves, meanwhile, fell from $104.8 billion in August to $99.5 billion in September, partly due to BSP foreign exchange operations, valuation adjustments, and government withdrawals. Still, those reserves are enough to cover 6.2 months of import.

blocks.text: How this affects businesses depends on which side of the dollar they sit.

Import-dependent manufacturers, retailers, airlines, and companies with unhedged dollar debt face higher costs. Exporters and business process outsourcing firms earning dollars while paying expenses in pesos could benefit from the exchange rate. Higher interest rates, meanwhile, make new borrowing and refinancing costlier, adding pressure to firms already struggling with input costs.

Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. says prolonged inflation may pose a greater threat to economic growth than higher interest rates, especially with household consumption accounting for around 70% of the economy.
Looking ahead, the November 9 third quarter 2026 GDP release will be the next measure to watch after economic growth slowed to a disappointing 2.3% in the second quarter of 2026.
Yet difficult economic conditions have not stopped companies from raising capital.

GCash parent Mynt completed the largest IPO in Philippine history on October 20, with the Philippine Stock Exchange reporting a P60.9-billion offering, including the overallotment. Meanwhile, Cebu-based Aznar Shipping is set to launch a smaller IPO of up to P737 million, targeting a December 18 listing to finance fleet and shipyard expansion.
We hope this readout helps inform your next strategy or boardroom decision. And as always, feel free to tell us what to tackle next, dear business leader. – Rappler.com

Readout is a new content series from data consultancy The Nerve, bringing you insights that bridge the gap between quick news headlines and dense technical reports. Readout tracks and explains business shifts in different Philippine industries. Crafted from on-the-ground reporting and data-driven analyses, Readout provides a clear read on where market and consumption are headed, what’s shaping demand across different sectors, who the key players are, and why it all matters.

articles.title: Edmonton and Calgary rejected her referendum. Does Danielle Smith have a city problem?
articles.summary: Nowhere in Alberta was the idea of a second referendum less popular than in urban centres. A year out from an election, Premier Danielle Smith says she's committed to identifying the issues important…

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith must contend with a sizable group of urban Albertans who appear to have rejected her latest political project, while she publicly spars with councillors over local issues such as zoning. (Sean Kilpatrick/Canadian Press)

blocks.text: This week the Alberta government pivots back to governing, with MLAs returning to the legislature for the first time since a contentious referendum on separation exposed the divide between, among other things, urban and rural Albertans.

Much of the pushback on the 10 referendum questions came from the province’s two largest centres. Calgary collectively voted "no" on all questions except proof of citizenship to vote, while Edmonton was a "no" across the board. Nowhere was the prospect of a second separation vote less popular.
“We all know there’s an urban-rural divide in Alberta politics,” says Lisa Young, a political scientist at the University of Calgary. “But the referendum results make it really stark.”

This presents a quandary for Premier Danielle Smith, who has historically been supported by — and focused her attention on — rural Alberta. Now, she must contend with a sizable group of urban Albertans who appear to have rejected her latest political project, while she publicly spars with councillors over local issues such as zoning.

Meanwhile, it remains to be seen whether her list of priorities for the upcoming sitting, which include public sector hiring based on "merit," protections for data centre development and the future of bike lanes, will speak to the cities.
“I think a lot of the recent focus on the more performative politics has served the UCP minority base really well,” said Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas on Tuesday.

“But the more we debate … which books should be in a library,” he said, referring to a recent bill to limit sexually explicit material in public libraries, “the more you lose the mainstream Calgarians who actually just want to get things done, want to know that life is safe and affordable.”

Smith herself has talked about the need to refocus on voters in Edmonton and Calgary, telling CBC News last week that her government needed to “identify the issues” that were important to residents of the two urban centres, which together make up just over half of the provincial population.

items: Danielle Smith has said no to a second referendum. But that decision might not be hers to make
Fight for independence won't end after referendum: Alberta Prosperity Project leader

blocks.text: Urban voters are focused on issues like education, health care and affordability, which is why her government has (temporarily) paused the gas tax at the pumps and rolled out “complexity teams” in classrooms, Smith said.

“The issues that were of the referendum, I think it’s pretty clear those are ... of greater interest to those who are in political parties and punditry circles and in rural Alberta than they were in Calgary or Edmonton."
Mapping out where Albertans voted to remain (or not) in Canada

It’s a change of script from 2022 when Smith, then a newly-minted party leader, made waves by suggesting she didn’t need much urban support. Instead, she had mapped out a “rural-based” path to electoral victory, telling a columnist that she’d done the math and would only need a relative handful of city seats if she won everywhere else.
Smith delivered, winning a majority the following year. She took a dozen seats in Calgary and a few on the outskirts of Edmonton, but painted most of the map blue everywhere else.
But Calgary has since rejected most of Smith’s referendum questions and, Young points out, flipped the reliably right-leaning riding of Calgary-Shaw to the NDP in a recent byelection.
“It looks like Calgary is in a different place than it was a couple of years ago,” Young said.

It may not help that Smith, a frequent critic of federal overreach, has waded into municipal issues in recent months, essentially overturning the decisions of city councils on issues like infill housing and zoning, and now appears to have her sights set on bike lanes, Young added.
It “doesn’t really signal wanting to have a relationship of respect with these urban governments,” she said.
“It’s going to be really interesting to watch and see whether there’s a softening of the hostility with Edmonton and Calgary city governments.”

Mayor Jeromy Farkas says he's not surprised most Calgarians rejected the referendum questions, and he will be looking to see how the provincial government prioritizes investment in his city over the next year. (Brendan Coulter/CBC)

But as Farkas points out, a year away from a provincial election, there’s still time for Smith to turn it around. He’s waiting to see what’s in the provincial budget: “I don’t watch what the politicians are saying; I watch what the politicians are doing.”
“We want to see much more substantive investment here locally in Calgary around affordability, public safety and essential infrastructure.”
The idea of Alberta as the land of cowboys and open prairie can clash with its urban reality as, contrary to stereotypes, Alberta is actually one of the country’s most urbanized provinces.

According to Statistics Canada, it had the third smallest proportion of rural residents as of 2021 at roughly 15 per cent. That makes it more urbanized than the national average, and close on the heels of uber-urban provinces like Ontario and British Columbia.

But rural issues play a big role in provincial politics here, Young notes. That’s in part a result of the electoral map, which allows for a smaller number of residents in some rural ridings, in order to ensure remote areas have adequate representation.

Drawing the map to ensure each riding has roughly the same number of people while making sure some don’t become unmanageably large is a longstanding struggle in Alberta. The report from the 2017 electoral boundary commission noted that at the time, the constituency of Lesser Slave Lake had a population of 28,858 people while Calgary-South East had 92,148.
In other words, a vote in Lesser Slave Lake had about three times the punch of a vote in Calgary.

But there’s also the consideration of the economic importance of rural areas, given the extent to which the actual action of key industries like oil and gas take place outside of urban centres, Young said.

History plays a role, too: “There’s a sense, historically, of people in rural communities seeing themselves as the authentic Albertans, the people who are generating value and prosperity for the province,” said Young.

The issues faced by urban and rural communities are actually not that different, but they show up in different ways, said Colin Aitchison, a former United Conservative press secretary who is now a managing director at communications and public affairs firm Enterprise Canada.
Whether it’s pressure from immigration or the need for jobs, the real challenge for governments is tailoring the message to respect the different ways each community is affected, he said.
“The policy solutions are going to be different, but the overarching issues are the same.”

Most of the priorities Smith’s government laid out for the new session were likely put in place before the referendum and do represent issues that are important to conservative voters regardless of where they live, Aitchison said.
But he expects to see Smith start speaking to a more general audience as the election approaches.

Under Jason Kenney, the United Conservative Party made inroads in Calgary, and could do so again, argues Colin Aitchison, a former press secretary who is now a managing director at Enterprise Canada. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Aitchison points to the 2019 election as an example of when the United Conservative message was heard loud and clear in the cities. That year, the party under Jason Kenney formed government with the help of most of the seats in Calgary and even a few on the outskirts of Edmonton.
“When [the UCP] made significant gains in Calgary, they focused on jobs, economy, pipelines,” he said. “A very simple message, and issues that resonate for both urban and rural communities.”

In interviews, Smith has pointed out that hers is not the only conservative government to struggle in urban areas. But Aitchison, who was involved with the campaign, said the recent victory of the B.C. Conservatives, in which they picked up seats even in parts of tony downtown Vancouver, shows that the UCP shouldn’t be counted out.
“[B.C. Conservatives] focused on affordability, they focused on pocketbook issues, jobs,” he said. “Those are issues that affect both rural and urban communities.”
For her part, Smith said she’s focused on cracking the urban code, to figuring out which issues are important to voters in Calgary and Edmonton and “prioritizing them in a serious way.”
“That’s what the job of politics is,” she said. “You’ve got to find out what’s bugging people and then you’ve got to focus on solving the problems,” she said. “I’m committed to doing that.”

articles.title: Carney to push for closer ties at Canada-EU summit in Montreal
articles.summary: The term "associate member" is reportedly off the table as officials discuss deeper economic and defence ties.

blocks.text: For decades, Canada-EU summits took place without much fanfare - but that's not the case for this coming two-day meeting in Montreal.
Thursday and Friday's summit will be closely watched for details on how Canada and the European bloc deepen their ties.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed "opening the door" to Canada for what she called an "associate membership" - a status that does not currently exist.

The overture came after Prime Minister Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, telling EU lawmakers that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
Carney and many EU member states welcome closer ties, but not all are on board with what to call this new relationship.
Some, like Germany, are questioning the "associate member" term, fearing that Canada is getting preferential treatment ahead of other nations who also want in.

According to reports by multiple news outlets, Germany and other nations successfully lobbied to remove mention of the title in a draft statement ahead of the summit, opting instead for softer language that references an "ever closer association".
Germany's ambassador to Canada, Matthias Lüttenberg, told CTV News on Tuesday that some member states were "a little surprised" by von der Leyen's announcement.
The concept of "associate membership", he added, is something that is not clearly understood as it pertains to Canada.

"Germany has been using the term of associate membership for something completely different, which is the relationship of the EU to Ukraine and potentially Moldova", he said, both of which have been trying to join the bloc for many years.
Lüttenberg noted, however, that neither Canada nor the EU is seeking full membership for the North American country.
Rather, both want to bring Canada "as close as possible" to the bloc without membership.
On the first day of the summit, Carney and von der Leyen and business leaders from both Europe and Canada will gather for a business forum.
Canadian officials said they also expect agreements to be hammered out on defence, critical minerals, research and trade over the two days.
Speaking to reporters earlier this week, European officials downplayed the possibility of a major announcement on Canada's new relationship with EU, saying much will be sorted in the coming months.

But both Canadian and EU officials have provided some clues on what the relationship could look like, including closer business ties and allowing more students to study on either side of the Atlantic.

Canada also does not plan on paying a membership fee similar to other EU nations, Canadian officials have said. Instead, it is looking at participating in different EU programmes that would benefit both Canada and member states.
And despite some disagreement about the wording, both have signalled they are fully on board with deepening ties.
"The wording is emblematic of the ambition," said one senior Canadian official who was granted anonymity to speak to reporters at a briefing ahead of the summit.

Since taking office last year, Prime Minister Carney has pushed Canada closer to Europe as his country continues to deal with an ongoing trade war with the US, its neighbour and largest trading customer.
US President Donald Trump has called the idea of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU "laughable", and has threatened "very serious tariffs" on Europe if he considered it a "hostile act".
Canadian officials stressed on Wednesday that their pivot to Europe is not meant to offend anybody, but rather to build on work that was already underway.
Canada recently signed an agreement that gives its defence companies procurement access to the EU's Security and Defence Partnership programme.
It also signed a landmark energy deal with Germany in May that would see the first-ever long-term shipments of liquified natural gas from Canada to Europe in the coming years.
Carney said earlier this week that the summit would "launch further formal discussions" between Canada and the EU on deepening ties and creating new opportunities for both sides.
As for what this new relationship status will be called, the prime minister said the "nomenclature" does not matter.
"What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians," he said.

articles.title: Who are the candidates short-listed for SC associate justice?
articles.summary: Marcos will pick his next SC associate justice appointee in place of retiring Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier

blocks.text: HIGHEST COURT. File photo of the Supreme Court of the Philippines.
Marcos will pick his next SC associate justice appointee in place of retiring Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier

items: The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) has shortlisted 11 candidates for the position of Supreme Court associate justice, in place of retiring Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier.
Public interviews for the candidates were conducted on October 13 and 15, with the shortlist transmitted to Malacañang for presidential appointment.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A total of 11 candidates have been short-listed by the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for the position of Supreme Court (SC) associate justice vice Associate Justice Amy Lazaro Javier, who will retire on November 16.
Here are the short-listed candidates in alphabetical order:

items: Court of Appeals (CA) Associate Justice Ramon M. Bato Jr.
Solicitor General Darlene Marie B. Berberabe
Commission on Audit Chairperson Gamaliel A. Cordoba
CA Associate Justice Ramon A. Cruz
CA Associate Justice Maria Elisa Sempio Diy
CA Associate Justice Myra V. Garcia-Fernandez
CA Presiding Justice Fernanda Lampas Peralta
Commission on Elections Commissioner Ernesto P. Maceda, Jr.
CA Associate Justice Ronaldo Roberto B. Martin
CA Associate Justice Walter S. Ong
Court of Tax Appeals Associate Justice Maria Rowena M. San Pedro

blocks.text: Under the 1987 Constitution, the JBC is mandated to screen applicants for the judiciary and the Office of the Ombudsman. After the screening, the JBC will conduct public interviews of the qualified candidates. A deliberation will follow, then the council will submit a short list to the president who will then make the appointment.

In this case, the JBC held the public interviews for the new candidates on October 13 and 15. It no longer interviewed bets who already went through the process since their interviews were still valid.

The judiciary is independent, but it is the president who is constitutionally mandated to make appointments to the courts. In this case, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will appoint his next justice to the High Court after Lazaro Javier reaches the mandatory age of 70 next month.
According to the SC, the short list has already been transmitted to Malacañang.

An SC justice must be a natural-born citizen, at least 40 years old, and have been a judge or law practitioner in the Philippines for at least 15 years or more. This is found under Section 7(1), Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution.

blocks.caption: Part 1: New candidates in the running to be Marcos’ 2nd SC justice
Part 2: Old-timer bets in the running to be Marcos’ 2nd SC justice

blocks.text: On top of this, a JBC 2020 rule states that an SC justice must serve a minimum of 2.5 years. This means that the eldest age of a candidate should be 67.5 years old, since the mandatory retirement age for justices is 70 years old.
On Thursday, the JBC also published the short list of chief justice nominees. These are the five candidates seeking to succeed Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo:

items: Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen
Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa
Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda
Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao
Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez

blocks.text: The chief justice and associate justice posts will be Marcos’ second and third appointee to the SC, which is currently dominated by appointees of former president Rodrigo Duterte. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Bernardo's ex-aide says he saw Jinggoy Estrada during delivery of boxes
articles.summary: A prosecution witness on Thursday said that he saw Senator Jinggoy Estrada when he delivered 12 boxes to him.

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 5:22pm
A prosecution witness on Thursday said that he saw Senator Jinggoy Estrada when he delivered 12 boxes to him.

Vergel Nino Garcia, former aide of state witness and ex-Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) undersecretary Roberto Bernardo, made the testimony during the hearing on the bail petition filed by suspended Senator Estrada amid a P573-million plunder case against him.
The case involves Estrada’s alleged receipt of kickbacks.
Garcia said that upon his delivery of 12 boxes for Estrada at the Artiaga Building in San Juan City in November 2024, he spotted Estrada in the same area wearing a t-shirt, pants and leather shoes.
Garcia said he did not see what was inside the boxes which he delivered upon the instructions of Bernardo.
After the delivery, Garcia said he called Bernardo to inform him that the delivery was made.
During the said delivery, Garcia also said he was accompanied by Bernardo’s driver, Francisco dela Fuente.

Aside from Estrada, Garcia said he also delivered boxes to former senator Bong Revilla, former Public Works secretary Manuel Bonoan (15 boxes), the late former DPWH Undersecretary Maria Catalina Cabral (one box and one paper bag) and former Education undersecretary Trygve Olaivar (eight suitcases and 15 boxes).
During the questioning by Estrada’s defense counsels, Garcia also said that they did not take photos or videos during the delivery.
A day earlier, Bernardo said there were four deliveries of commitments or kickbacks to Estrada from 2024 to 2025, but he was only present for one delivery in June 2025.
Bernardo later said it wasn’t easy for him to implicate Senator Jinggoy Estrada whom he accused of receiving kickbacks from government projects.
Bernardo made such position when asked as to why he did not implicate Estrada in his earlier affidavit.

“During that time [of my first affidavit], I have no confirmation, I have no solid evidence that will prove [his involvement]. I have already in [my] mind that he is a proponent [of projects], but I have to confirm [first],” Bernardo said.
“Ang hirap po ipahamak ang kaibigan. Hindi ko po kaagad magagawa iyon. Kailangan may solid evidence po," Bernardo added.
(It is tough to betray a friend. I cannot do that easily. I need to have solid evidence.)

Bernardo also pointed out that his previous affidavit, made prior to 2026, provides that given the complexities in the case, he reserved his right to “execute a supplemental affidavit if warranted.” — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Audacious Indian jailbreak saga ends with 17 prisoners recaptured
articles.summary: The jailbreak began with a fake seizure and ended 36 hours later with all the inmates back behind bars.

blocks.text: A fake medical emergency, an audacious jailbreak and a 36-hour search operation that ended with 17 prisoners being recaptured.
Those are the highlights of a story from India's Tamil Nadu state that has captured headlines across the country.
It began on Monday night after 17 men escaped from a prison in Theni district in the southern state after overpowering guards, and ended almost two days later with police catching them in batches.

The incident has drawn attention to overcrowding in Indian prisons. Police say the Theni prison was housing 334 inmates against a capacity of 200, leaving authorities unable to maintain control once chaos broke out.
The state police said it has suspended nine staff at the prison for alleged negligence in connection with the incident.
All the men who escaped were undertrials - inmates on trial or awaiting one - and 18 of them were in one cell at the prison in Thekkampatti in Theni.

On Monday night at 2230 local time (17:00 GMT), one of the prisoners acted like he was going through a seizure. The other cellmates shouted for help and a jail official responded. He was soon overpowered by the prisoners, police said.

The prisoners then got out of the cell, reportedly attacked two other jail guards and took away keys which they used to open the main gate and flee. While 17 escaped, one returned to the prison immediately.
Several prison personnel were injured in the attack.

items: The 'mastermind' behind India's biggest jailbreak

blocks.text: Police sources told BBC Tamil that they were examining the possibility of collusion between some prison officials and the escaped men.
Sandeep Rathore, Director General of Police for Prisons in Tamil Nadu, said in a press briefing that the jailbreak was caused by "human error".
"There was a clear breach of security protocol as the prisoners managed to pass through a three-tier barrier manned by security personnel," he said.

At the time of the incident, only four guards were on duty, far below the staffing required to maintain the prescribed 1:6 guard-to-inmate ratio recommended by the state - which should have worked out to 34 guards against the approved strength of 200 prisoners.
The police then launched a manhunt, calling forces from across the state.
"Advanced technology, drone surveillance, CCTV footage analysis, and the tireless efforts of police personnel played a crucial role," the department said in a statement on X.
Four men were arrested at a bus station in a nearby village, and the fifth was caught while he was travelling in a tuk-tuk.

A drone search of a forest near the prison led to eight more escaped prisoners being caught. Videos of the arrests showed the men obeying police instructions even as they did not answer questions from reporters who were also seen at the scene.
Two more were captured with the help of drone surveillance, police said, while the last two men surrendered on Wednesday.
News agency PTI reported that all 17 recaptured prisoners have been moved to high-security correctional prisons.
Rathore told media that all prisons across the state would be audited to check if rules were being followed.

The incident evoked memories of one of the biggest jailbreaks in Tamil Nadu in 1995 when 43 suspected militants escaped from a special camp after digging a 153-foot-long tunnel beneath a historic fort. Some of them were never recaptured.

While the investigation is going on, the incident has sparked a conversation on overcrowding in Indian prisons. The National Crime Records Bureau's last Prison Statistics India report from 2023 showed a national occupancy rate of 120.1%.

Data shows that undertrial prisoners - individuals who are detained while they await police investigation or court trials - make up more than 73% of India's total prison population. Human rights groups and legal experts have also raised concerns about delays in investigations and trials that lead to people languishing for years behind bars.
Additional reporting by Siraj and Prabhurao Anandhan

The North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) is expecting a surge in passengers starting Friday afternoon, October 30 as Filipinos go on exodus in observance of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day this weekend.

“Ito po ay ine-expect natin mga bukas ng hapon, early afternoon po siguro. Tuloy-tuloy po yan hanggang gabi. And then early morning po ng Saturday hanggang hapon na po siguro ng Saturday, 'Yun po 'yung ating pa-norte,” said NLEX Corporation AVP for Traffic Operations Robin Ignacio in an interview with Balitanghali.

(We are expecting this around tomorrow afternoon, probably early afternoon. That will continue until night. And then early morning on Saturday until probably Saturday afternoon—that's for our northbound traffic.)
The NLEX official said that traffic along the expressway is still fastmoving, especially going north.

“Baka hindi naman po gano'n kaano po 'yung difference ano, pero pa from 'yung ating normal daily average, ine-expect po namin na maaari po itong tataas ng between 3 to 5% ito pong period ng today, October 29 hanggang November 3,” said Ignacio.
(The difference might not be that huge, but compared to our normal daily average, we expect that it could rise between 3% to 5% during this period from today, October 29, until November 3.)

“Pero siyempre, meron po tayong 'yung mga peak hours na sinasabi po namin kagaya nung nabanggit ko po kanina 'yung dagsa. Maaari pong 'yung hourly traffic po natin no'n kompara sa normal daily, normal hourly traffic natin eh baka magiging mas mahigit pa po ng 20% 'yung itataas nung peak hours na 'yon,” he added.

(But of course, we have what we call peak hours, just like the surge I mentioned earlier. Our hourly traffic then, compared to our normal daily or normal hourly traffic, might increase by more than 20% during those peak hours.)
Further, NLEX said that it has already deployed around 1,500 personnel starting today.
“Tinataya po namin nasa mga 1,500 personnel mula po sa mga toll tellers po natin, mga patrol, security, traffic marshal at saka 'yung ating incident response teams,” said Ignacio.
(We estimate around 1,500 personnel, ranging from our toll tellers, patrols, security, traffic marshals, to our incident response teams.) — RSJ, GMA News

Malacañang on Thursday defended anew the P50 million bounty set on Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa’s head, saying that his world has gotten smaller as authorities have stepped up efforts to arrest him.

“Totoo na lumiliit ang mundo ni Senator Bato dahil ang maaaring makakita sa kaniya ay magbibigay ng impormasyon agad-agad sa PNP at sa ibang law enforcement agencies,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in a press briefing.

articles.title: Audio reveals exchanges between control centre and drivers before deadly Spain train crash
articles.summary: The recordings appear to show one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another up ahead had stalled.

blocks.text: Audio recordings published in Spanish media reveal conversations between train drivers and a railway control centre in the minutes leading up to a deadly train crash that killed at least 68 people and injured dozens.
Officials are investigating the cause of the disaster, which occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train on Wednesday morning.

Three audio recordings between the control centre in Madrid and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another some 25km (15 miles) up ahead had stalled.
The release of the recordings comes as Spain begins three days of national mourning for one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history.
One train, run by state-owned operator Renfe, had 397 passengers on board. Ahead of it on the same line was a train run by private operator Iryo, with 147 passengers.
A reported issue with the automatic signalling system - a computer failure - had forced all trains to halt on the affected stretch.
But later the Renfe train was ordered to proceed in "error", according to Spain's transport minister.

Audio recordings published by Spanish news outlets including El Pais and RTVE reveal the conversations that took place between the two train's drivers and the control centre in the Spanish capital ahead of the crash.
In one recording, a control centre operator tells the Renfe driver to resume its journey at normal speed after some technical issues.
"Continue your journey and then proceed under [Lateral Signalling Block], at normal speed with normal operation," the control centre operator says to the driver.
The driver replies, "At normal speed?" To which the controller says: "Yes."
The Lateral Signaling Block is a back-up or alternative train system used when the automatic signalling or data transmission system fails.
Later, the driver of the other Iryo train says in another audio recording that communication with the train-control system has been lost and they are stationary at Urda.
The train "is stationary in front of the entry signal at Urda", the driver tells the control centre operator. After a series of exchanges, the driver is then told to "resume the journey" normally.

The Iryo driver then contacts the control centre again, according to a later recording, saying they cannot start the train. "The train won't allow me to control the [security] system. That's why I am still stopped in front of the entry signal," they say.
The latter recording suggests that the controller had been notified that the Iryo train remained stationary as the Renfe train approached.
Iryo said its train, which had 147 passengers on board, was "struck from behind" by another train, by Renfe train which was carrying 397 passengers.
Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente said on Wednesday that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said the "whole of Spain is grieving", adding that "lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense".
Emergency crews worked through the night under powerful floodlights to cut open metal carriages in the search for victims, with many of those killed in the crash still to be identified.

Hundreds of personnel have been deployed to the disaster site to assist with recovery efforts, according to Spain's interior ministry, with drones and helicopters being used to find victims and remove rubble.
Witnesses described seeing people crying and bleeding, passengers trapped in their seats and smoke billowing throughout the carriages, one of which caught fire.

Sánchez said it was "unacceptable" that Spain had suffered two serious rail disasters this year, after a high-speed crash killed 46 people near Córdoba in January. It occurred on the same line as Wednesday's accident, but much further south.
Most political parties suspended campaigning for upcoming elections following the incident.

The exception was the far-right party Vox. Its leader, Santiago Abascal, said his party would not take part in what he described as attempts to "use mourning to silence criticism" of the country's rail infrastructure.

articles.title: Healey accused of a ‘complete failure’ to target energy bill support at those most in need – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Resolution Foundation says ‘poorest half of households will gain… just £14 more than the £144 received by the richest half’

Good morning. The day after the budget is often the moment when…

blocks.text: Good morning. The day after the budget is often the moment when big initiatives announced by the chancellor the day before with a flourish start to unravel as experts pore over the small print. There is not much of that happening this morning – mainly because John Healey did not have any really big initiatives up his sleeve. Compared with a normal budget, his tax and spending initiatives were mostly relatively minor. That means that the opposition parties have been struggling to find things to attack, and so instead they have resorted to criticising Healey for what he did not do: slash welfare (the Tory/Reform UK solution), or join the EU’s single market (the Lib Dems’).

Healey has given interviews to all the main broadcasters, which are playing out this morning, but they were recorded last night and they don’t have any sensational new revelations. As Rowena Mason reports, one of the top lines was Healey saying he would cut welfare spending before the election.
But there were other lines in the interviews too. I will be posting all the highlights this morning.

The two main public spending thinktanks, the Institute for Fiscal Studies and the Resolution Foundation, are both publishing reports assessing the budget this morning. The RF has issued a news release with its main findings and its assessment of the overall economic impact of the budget measures highlights three problems.

items: It accuses Healey of a “complete failure” to target help with energy bills at those most in need. It says:

blocks.text: double quotation markThe poorest half of households will gain £158 on average from cost of living support this year and next, just £14 more than the £144 received by the richest half – highlighting a complete failure to target help at those who need it most.

items: It says long-term public spending plans imply a return to austerity. It says:

blocks.text: double quotation markTight spending plans beyond 2028-29 imply departmental budgets will take more of the strain in the future. But if the 3% defence target is met and real health spending continues to grow at 2.6%, pencilled-in spending totals imply that funding for 13 ‘unprotected’ departments will fall to just 4.7% of GDP by 2031-32, close to the post-austerity historic low.

items: It says people will get poorer between now and the end of the parliament. It says:

blocks.text: double quotation markMedian real annual disposable incomes for working age households are set to grow by a paltry £600 over the course of the parliament. Worse still, those gains are already behind us. Between now (2026-27) and the end of the parliament (2028-29), typical incomes are forecast to fall in total by £1,050 (3 per cent).

This is one reason why so many people continue to think Andy Burnham will call an election next spring (before the electorate feels the full misery of getting poorer) – despite Burnham yesterday saying he would not hold one within the next 12 months.
Here is the agenda for the day.
9am: Jonathan Haskel, chair of the Office for Budget Responsibility, and Ruth Curtice, head of the Resolution Foundation, speak at an event where the RF is presenting its budget analysis.
9.30am: Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
10.30am: Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, presents the IFS’s budget analysis.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 11.30am: MPs resume the budget debate in the Commons.
Lunchtime: Andy Burnham is on a visit to a Rolls-Royce factory in the Midlands where he is speaking to the media.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Rising water is forcing this French town off Newfoundland to move. Not everyone is ready to leave
articles.summary: "We are not safe from climate risks that could cause danger to people and property," the mayor says.

image.caption: Most of the town of Miquelon sits on a low stretch of gravel and sand, just one to two metres above sea level, making it vulnerable to rising water levels and violent storms. (Jean-Christophe Paulau/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
"We are not safe from climate risks that could cause danger to people and property," the mayor says.
New homes under construction as Miquelon tries to save itself from climate change
For two centuries, being close to the water has been good for the town of Miquelon.
Fishing on the ocean provided a livelihood, and made it easy to travel.
But now, the ocean has become the town’s biggest threat.

"The village is built on sand and gravel about two metres above sea level," said the town's mayor Franck Detcheverry, speaking in French. "We are not safe from climate risks that could cause danger to people and property."
The island is French territory but just a 90-minute ferry ride away from Newfoundland.
Lines on the siding of the customs office at the harbour show what higher ocean levels and worse storms could mean.
A line on the customs office in Miquelon shows the predicted water level of the ocean at the end of the century. (Peter Cowan/CBC)
A mark at 3.7 metres above sea level shows a prediction of how high water could get during intense storms by the end of the century.
It would inundate the town.
Hurricane Fiona was a big wake up call, narrowly missing the island before slamming into Newfoundland, where around 100 homes were washed away or badly damaged in Port aux Basques.
The mayor worries it’s only a matter of time before disaster strikes his community.
Franck Detcheverry, the mayor of Miquelon, says moving the community will ensure his town survives climate change. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)
The plan to move
This is why the town is moving to higher ground.
New building lots are being developed on the other side of the harbour, less than a kilometre away from the existing town.

"Rebuilding houses on a safe site allows people peace of mind, knowing they can pass their home to their children and grandchildren," said Detcheverry. "Miquelon can endure in the future, which is no longer the case today in the current village."
Right now, almost a dozen homes are starting to go up.
The plan is voluntary.
France’s Barnier Fund buys people’s homes, giving them the money they need to build on the new lots.
When they move in, their old house will be torn down, and no new structures will be allowed on the site.
As the the new village goes up, the old one comes down.
About a dozen new homes are under construction on the new town site, less than a kilometre from the current town. (Katie Breen/CBC)
Some don’t want to move
But not everyone is welcoming the idea.
"The idea of completely relocating the village doesn’t seem like a good idea to us," said Maryline Detcheverry, also speaking in French, about her petition raising concerns about the plan.
Detcheverry is a common last name in the town — she’s not related to the mayor.
She’s worried that they’re giving up on the current town too easily.
"The first and most essential thing is to protect what exists. We must protect what is currently there. That means doing some work to strengthen the east side of the village of Miquelon."
Miquelon moving residents’ homes due to rising sea levels
For some, it’s too late to move.
Michel Detcheverry, who is also not related to the mayor, is in his late 60s. He’s lived in his house his whole life, and his late uncle helped him renovate it.
It has memories.
"To just take everything, tear everything down and go somewhere else, I don't feel like it," he said.
Michel Detcheverry has lived in his house his entire life. He says he’s too old to start over with a new house. (Peter Cowan/CBC)
It will be hard to see neighbours move and a village that’s existed for 200 years start to change.
"It's going to be difficult to see because you're going to see that village disappear, slowly," he said.
This is the first time France has moved an entire village.
It will slowly happen over the next few decades.

items: Memorial University ends Frecker program in St. Pierre after more than 50 years
Canada, France pledge to work together on space infrastructure, economy

blocks.text: On a recent trip to the island, French President Emanuel Macron promised 20 million euros to help build new lots — room for 75 new houses, about half of what they figure they’ll eventually need.
The mayor understands why not everyone wants to move.

"For some, it's a loss of identity, and some people feel they are losing their bearings and their family heritage," he said. "I'm attached to Miquelon Island, but not necessarily to the current site."
People who don’t want to move worry what will happen to the current town as some people move out and their old homes are destroyed. (Katie Breen/CBC)

articles.title: Ethiopia acquires Russian fighter jets and air defence systems amid war in Tigray
articles.summary: The acquisition of the warplanes comes amid ongoing fighting in northern Tigray region that started last month.

blocks.text: Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity.

He said Ethiopia and Russia agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow.
The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats.

Abiy, who described Russian President Vladimir Putin, "as a close friend of Ethiopia", said Ethiopia had now become the first country in sub‑Saharan Africa to own this kind of "advanced combat technology."
"If we fail to build this capability, surviving as a country in our region will become difficult. Countries with sufficient preparation are not easily defied," he said.
Russia and Ethiopia have signed several military agreements in recent years, including a deal in 2021 to train and improve technology for the military.
Abiy explained that Ethiopia signed an agreement with Russia several years ago to procure the Su‑35 jets and S‑400 systems, citing global air force trends and security threats facing the country.
The Su‑35, he noted, is equipped for both air‑to‑air and air‑to‑ground combat, with the ability to detect and neutralize incoming cruise missiles at distances of up to 200 kilometers.

Military intelligence analyst Qalaab Segatu told BBC Amharic that Ethiopia's acquisition of additional warplanes was a key indication that "it was preparing for possible wars with other countries, not just internal conflicts".
According to him, the jets are highly maneuverable and capable of covering large areas, with radars capable of ensuring air superiority and long-range scanning.

When combined, the fighter jets and air defence systems "create a significant capability to protect and defend major cities and critical infrastructure such as the Renaissance Dam, providing key strategic air superiority," Qalaab said.
Abiy said besides the advanced capabilities of the aircraft from Russia, the use of drones was equally important in strengthening deterrence.
Ethiopia has extensively used military drones, including those sourced from Turkey and China, in recent conflicts.
"We need to build capacity not only with drones, but also with the fourth generation capabilities of the Su 30 and Su 35 [aircraft]," Abiy said.

The latest acquisition of military hardware from Russia comes after the current conflict in northern Tigray started last month between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended a civil war.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing the TPLF, which it denies.
Tensions between the two countries have also persisted as Abiy terms Ethiopia's lack of direct sea access an "existential question", which Eritrea views as a direct threat to its sovereignty.
Eritrea gained independence in 1993 after a decades-long war with Ethiopia, with the latter losing access to the sea.

articles.title: PNP reiterates call for Bato dela Rosa's surrender as deadline nears
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Thursday reiterated its appeal for Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa to surrender as the deadline set by the Department of the Interior and Local Government…

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 4:21pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) on Thursday reiterated its appeal for Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa to surrender as the deadline set by the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) nears.
“Again, the same appeal that we are giving to him and his family. Let's end this with dignity on your part,” PNP spokesperson Police Colonel Allen Rae Co said during a press briefing.
Co said authorities want to avoid any violent encounters, injuries, or deaths during the ongoing manhunt for the senator.

“Let's avoid any untoward incidents, any potential dangerous encounters, or any harm that may come to anybody. We would like to avoid any injuries, any violent encounters, and of course, pinakamasama na po is mayroon pong masawi dito sa (worst, fatalities in the) operation,” he said.
The one-week deadline given by the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) for Dela Rosa to surrender expires on Friday.
Co declined to disclose specific details of its manhunt operations as this could compromise the efforts of police personnel and put them in danger.
He noted that authorities are not expecting wanted individuals to remain in one place. For him, intensified operations and the announcement of a reward could restrict Dela Rosa's movements.
The government has offered a P50-million reward for information that could lead to the senator's location and arrest.

Co clarified that the reward is intended for individuals who can provide tips or information to authorities, and not for civilians to personally arrest the senator or take the law into their own hands.
Dela Rosa, a former PNP chief, is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in connection with the crimes against humanity case arising from former President Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs.
The senator is accused of being a co-perpetrator in the alleged crimes.
The DILG earlier claimed that Dela Rosa was hiding in Mindanao under the protection of an “armed and powerful group,” but did not identify the group. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: EJK victims' families hold Mass for Undas 2026
articles.summary: Families of the victims of extrajudicial killings during the Duterte administration gathered for a Mass in Quezon City on Thursday ahead of the Undas.

blocks.text: Published October 29, 2026 4:16pm
Families of the victims of extrajudicial killings during the Duterte administration gathered for a Mass in Quezon City on Thursday ahead of the Undas.
In a Balitanghali report, GMA's Sandra Aguinaldo said the families gathered at the Christ the King church.
Led by staunch drug war critic Father Flavie Villanueva, the Mass was part of a program meant for healing.
Villanueva said that this has been a yearly activity to help the families rise from the grief they experienced over the death of their loved ones.

However, the priest reminded the families that justice is also needed to help them move on. This is why they continue to monitor Duterte’s case at the International Criminal Court (ICC) at the Hague, Netherlands.
Duterte is being tried for crimes against humanity in relation to the drug war, which killed at least 6,000 people.
Villanueva said that it is also hard for the families to move on if the drug war deaths kept being denied.
During the part of the Mass where people say “peace be with you,” participants were encouraged to embrace one another instead.

Many of the mothers weeped during this part. The participants of the Mass said that such activities helped them heal from the pain of losing their loved ones to the drug war. —Jean Mangaluz/AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Hello Kitty company cuts ties with Japanese spy show after China outcry
articles.summary:
Sanrio ends association with TV drama Vivant after China says portrayal of ruthless Chinese agents is ‘deliberate smear’

The company behind the successful

blocks.text: The company behind the successful Hello Kitty franchise has apologised and ended its commercial tie-up with a Japanese TV drama after Chinese state media and netizens condemned the show’s “deliberate smears” against China.

Sanrio, a Japanese firm whose characters are popular around the world, said in a post on the Chinese social media site Weibo that it had decided to end its association with the TV drama Vivant after concluding that it “contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio’s core values”.
In the second season of the popular spy thriller, produced by the Japanese TBS network, Masato Sakai plays a salaryman who is drawn into a web of international crime and espionage.

The backlash began this week when Chinese state media blasted the portrayal of Chinese agents using “ruthless violence” to torture members of a secret unit of Japan’s self-defence forces, calling it a “deliberate smear” against Beijing.
Chinese media said that some of the torture methods were similar to those Japanese troops used against Chinese civilians during the second world war.

The state-run tabloid Global Times said the acts shown in the episode “bear striking similarities to the torture inflicted on Chinese nationals by invading Japanese troops” during the war, adding that the drama “distorts the truth by attributing these atrocities to modern Chinese characters”.
In the 4 October episode, a Chinese agent is seen cutting off the fingers of the Japanese intelligence officer and stabbing him in the abdomen.

Sanrio said in a statement: “Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people.
“We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects.”
The drama’s first season, set in a fictional central Asian country, avoided controversy, but its latest season is being shown at a time of increasingly fractious relations between Beijing and Tokyo.

Japan’s conservative prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, set off a diplomatic row in November last year when she told MPs that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could trigger the deployment of her country’s self-defence forces if the conflict posed an existential threat to Japan.
Takaichi said earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and hoped to watch them over the year-end and new year holidays.
China is a crucial overseas market for Sanrio, whose cast of characters includes My Melody and Cinnamoroll – both featured in Vivant-themed merchandise.
The Tokyo-based company racked up 781m yuan ($117m) in revenue from the Chinese market in the first half of this year, according to Chinese media, up more than 40% from the same period last year.

The backlash against Sanrio comes days after the French international footballer Kylian Mbappé was dropped by several Chinese brands after he jokingly referred to Mao Zedong as a “dictator”. The Real Madrid forward, who is nicknamed the “dictator” for his influence on the game, later apologised for his “ill-judged” remarks.

articles.title: More Canadian provinces are ending time changes. What does it mean for your health?
articles.summary: Researchers are raising concerns as parts of Canada move to permanent daylight time, warning that later winter sunrises could have consequences for sleep and health.

image.caption: Clock at Charlottetown City Hall in Charlottetown, P.E.I. As parts of Canada stop changing their clocks twice a year, sleep scientists say the time they choose to keep could have consequences for sleep and health. (Shane Ross/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New
Researchers are raising concerns as parts of Canada move to permanent daylight time, warning that later winter sunrises could have consequences for sleep and health.
Sleep scientists say ending the switch is good, but permanent daylight is the wrong choice

Millions of Canadians will turn their clocks back one hour this weekend, while millions of others will not. This divide is putting Canadians under different time systems — with potentially different consequences for their health.

Most of British Columbia, as well as Alberta, Manitoba and the Northwest Territories are no longer changing their clocks twice a year, joining Yukon and most of Saskatchewan. Most of Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces will still turn their clocks back on Nov. 1 for the end of daylight saving time.

For Quebec, this could be the last time. Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon announced Wednesday that his government is moving to end the twice-yearly clock change, but it has not yet decided which time the province will keep. He said that decision will be made after consulting experts.

Research suggests permanent standard time — the time we return to in the fall — is more closely aligned with the body's internal clock than permanent daylight time, which several provinces have chosen.
Here's what winter time would look like across Canada under proposed time-zone changes

Joseph De Koninck, an emeritus professor of psychology at the University of Ottawa, has studied sleep for decades. He said the springtime change is the most problematic because people lose an hour of sleep when they set their clocks forward, creating a mismatch between the body's internal biological clock and solar time.

De Koninck explained that our biological clock uses light to synchronize itself. As daylight changes with the seasons, our circadian rhythms adjust gradually. Making a one-hour adjustment all at once, however, is much more difficult.
"We are able to adapt, but it's not optimal for our health."
The Edmonton skyline at dawn. As one of Canada's northernmost major cities, Edmonton will see winter sunrises as late as 10 a.m. under Alberta's new permanent daylight time. (John Robertson/CBC)
Why morning light matters
Michael Antle, head of the University of Calgary's psychology department and a professor who studies circadian rhythms, said permanent standard time would have been better for Alberta.
Because of the province's northern latitude and position within its time zone, it already has late winter sunrises, Antle said. Permanent daylight time will push them forward another hour.
"It's not the choice I would have made," he said of the province's decision.
Antle said daylight time essentially means society has agreed to get up and go to work or school an hour earlier.
Most people's circadian clocks run slightly slow, making them somewhat "night owlish," he said. Morning light helps speed up that clock.
Michael Antle, a University of Calgary psychology professor, says permanent standard time is healthier because it better aligns with people's body clocks. (Submitted by Michael Antle)
When morning light arrives later, there can be a mismatch between what the body wants to do and what work or school requires.
Antle described this effect as "social jetlag."

Antle pointed to population studies that found people exposed to later sunsets slept less and had higher rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease. He also cited Russian research that found winter depression among young people increased while Russia observed permanent daylight time.
Why some scientists don't support B.C.'s switch to permanent daylight time
Why researchers say permanent daylight time is a bad idea
Both researchers distinguish between the disruption caused by changing the clocks and the effects of living on daylight time year-round.

Antle said the spring change creates a sudden shift that can leave people feeling as though they're living on the wrong time for several weeks. Permanent daylight time would extend that mismatch through the darkest months of the year.
He would prefer permanent standard time. Continuing to spring forward and fall back would be a compromise, he said, preserving later summer evenings without the longer-term winter mismatch.

items: For thousands of workers, lifelong time-zone math will go out the window when B.C. stops changing clocks
Time zones in Canada are getting complicated. These maps lay them out

blocks.text: Night owls who work regular daytime jobs may struggle the most because they already find it difficult to wake up early, Antle said.

Those darker mornings are also having a real-world impact. Ski hills in Alberta's Bow Valley, for example, are delaying their opening times this winter to give staff more daylight to prepare the slopes before skiers arrive.
But most schools and workplaces have less flexibility to change their hours based on when the sun is up.
Changing clocks twice a year a question of public health: prof
Canada becomes a natural experiment
Canada's emerging patchwork could give researchers an opportunity to study neighbouring populations living under different time systems.
Antle said he would have preferred a year's notice to collect baseline data before Alberta made the change.
He said researchers should examine mental health, vehicle and pedestrian collisions, school performance and attendance, and workplace attendance and tardiness.
De Koninck noted that researchers now have tools to document sleep habits over time and compare how people adapt in different provinces.

But he expects Western Canadians may make their feelings known before researchers have years of data to analyze. People may not fully understand what permanent daylight time means, he said, until they've experienced a winter with much later sunrises.
"Those who've tried it haven't liked it," he said.
For De Koninck, the larger concern is what prolonged sleep disruption can mean for people's health.
"If you feel sleep deprived, then you have a host of issues, psychological and physical," he said.
"You can't play with your sleep."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eric Michael Johnson is a senior writer and editor based in Vancouver. Before joining CBC, he was an award-winning science writer and editor. He holds a PhD in the history of science from the University of British Columbia. He can be reached at eric.johnson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Hello Kitty maker cuts ties with Japanese spy drama after China backlash
articles.summary: Sanrio has apologised after its merchandise line with Japanese TV series Vivant drew criticism.

blocks.text: Sanrio, the company behind Hello Kitty, has apologised and ended its merchandise partnership with a controversial Japanese TV show after drawing backlash in China.

Vivant, a popular spy thriller, has been widely slammed in Chinese state media and by Chinese social media users for its depiction of Chinese agents using brutal torture tactics on a Japanese operative.
The criticism has extended to the internationally beloved Hello Kitty and her friends, including My Melody and Cinnamoroll, who were featured in merchandise dressed as characters from the show.
Sanrio said it terminated its collaboration with Vivant after determining that it "contained elements inconsistent with Sanrio's core values".

"Since its inception, Sanrio has consistently used its characters to convey values such as care and connection, and remains committed to its corporate philosophy of fostering harmony among all people," Sanrio said in the statement late on Wednesday.
"We take the feedback we have received regarding this incident very seriously. Moving forward, we will strengthen our review processes for all future collaborative projects."
China-Japan ties have plunged to their lowest point in years, since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments on Taiwan last November sparked a diplomatic firestorm.
Responding to a question in parliament, Takaichi suggested that Japan would activate its self-defence force if China attacked Taiwan.
Beijing has since been heaping pressure on Tokyo, from restricting rare earth exports to curbing tourism and even reclaiming its pandas.
Takaichi told parliament earlier this month that she had recorded episodes of Vivant and planned to watch them over the year-end holidays.
State-run Global Times took aim at Sanrio on Wednesday, saying the hugely popular cat character "should not dance with Japan's right wing".

Sanrio "stands to lose far more than short-term sales" by collaborating with "anti-China content", the Global Times article said. "The trust and emotional bond it has built up over a long time will also suffer."

When asked about Sanrio's scrapped partnership with Vivant on Thursday, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry said the incident should "serve as a warning to the international community and discerning people in Japan".

articles.title: Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany's health scare highlights the need for better support for elite coaches
articles.summary: Vincent Kompany’s health concern is a reminder that elite football's pressures affect coaches too. Better support, clearer structures and mental health safeguards are increasingly vital.

image.caption: Bayern fans made a banner for Vincent Kompany that read "Get well soon Vincent, we are with you!"Image: Bernd Feil/M.i.S./IMAGO

blocks.text: Vincent Kompany has just returned home from hospital. The Bayern Munich head coach admitted that he hadn't listened to his body, "and then at some point, my body just said, 'Enough is enough!'"

Bayern Munich's sporting director Max Eberl, who left Gladbach in 2022 due to his own health concerns, told German public broadcaster ARD that the 40-year-old Belgian had been suffering from meningeal irritation, which if untreated can become meningitis.
"They found out what it is. It is a meningeal irritation that brought on the incident last Friday," said Eberl, referring to when Kompany collapsed during training and required an emergency doctor.
"Honestly, he is doing as well as can be expected. He has been discharged from hospital today, which is the biggest and best news for all of us."

blocks.caption: Vincent Kompany's illness has seen a large amount of support from the coaching communityImage: Markus Ulmer/Ulmer/Teamfoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: The news has been met by great concern from the German football community. Bayern fans held a banner showing their support, many German media outlets wrote opinion articles softly reminding that coaches are humans too and they too need support. Even the wider coaching community has started to ask questions.
"It’s something you take to heart and think about," Freiburg head coach Julian Schuster said after his team lost to Bayern recently.
"We coaches aren’t always very good at taking care of ourselves in those situations."
Why do coaches push themselves too hard?

Kompany, whose father became the first Black mayor in Belgium after moving there from the DR Congo, has faced an enormous amount of adversity in his life. At just 14, his parents divorced and he told The Guardian in a 2019 interview: "I need to be fed stuff constantly, otherwise I don’t know how to function. I can't remember a lazy Sunday."

The Belgian's own history, both in his childhood and as former professional player, also plays a role in understanding the challenges coaches face. It is also telling that Aaron Danks, Kompany's assistant coach, admitted that "getting Vince to rest is a challenge."

"I think we (coaches) have a really poor measure of ourselves within this example of like, wasn't listening to my body. I think a lot of coaches are really poor at that," coaching mentor Cody Royle, who has worked with teams in the NBA and the Premier League, told DW.

"And so part of my role is to enhance their attunement to that, to ask questions to that effect, to try to perhaps even impart some things that I've learned along the way or heard from others or other coaches that are going through similar things so that you can actually start to put words to what that feeling might have been or where you maybe touched burnout but it didn't quite get there and you're able to rescue something and start to really develop skill within it," he said.

"I think with Vincent's example we also need to account for the fact that this is a young man still finding his way in coaching and so he's still understanding what those triggers are within his body and what they're really telling him Maybe he had physical things that he could read when he was playing. These are more mental triggers, and he's still learning that and that's part of what he needs to do. But there should be people around that help."
Coaches in need of more support
It begs the question, in 2026, at a time when awareness around mental and physical health is greater than ever, particularly in elite sport, how is this still possible?
"I suspect that many head coaches aren't able to let go or delegate," Frank Wormuth, an educator for the German Football Association (DFB), told DW.
"They want to control everything because they don't feel secure when the team loses," continued Wormuth, adding that that's why coaches often bring close friends into their staff.
"You'd think professional coaches wouldn't have to worry, since they've earned enough money, but that’s not a good coach's priority—success is far more important."

blocks.caption: Frank Wormuth (left) also had moments where he realized football had taken overImage: Pro Shots/IMAGO

blocks.text: A former coach, Wormuth admits that he had moments in his career when he had lost sight of how much of a role football was playing in his life.
"I never felt like I was doing too much until my kids pointed out to me—when I was at home—that I wasn't the coach anymore, but should be fulfilling the role of a father," Wormuth said.
"That's when I realized that I was truly operating 24/7 as a coach in my head, even when I was at home."
German football identity: Frank Wormuth
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio
Royle believes coaches need to learn more about how to manage themselves.
"I kind of throw my hands up a little bit at the fact that we aren't further along," Royle said.
"We're not even trying to educate this in to our young coaches as they come through. The education system probably facilitates this as much as the organizations that are individually responsible."
Will change come to coaching?

Clearly, if not well managed, extremely demanding elite-sports environments with high expectations on individuals makes for a dangerous combination. Both Wormuth and Royle advocate for the concept of a second set of eyes.
"Maybe it is that there's a mechanism now for coaches to really investigate," Royle said.

Having someone who sits outside the organization and doesn't belong to the politics to be able to —whether it's on the phone or come in for a visit — just say, 'You need to go home because this isn't going well.'"

"This is a game where Jock Stein literally dropped dead on the sideline, right? There shouldn't need to be any more conversation beyond that... and it was workaholism and stress that caused it," added Royle.
"So I don't know what else it's going to take, but I just don't think the game really cares enough to change anything about it. The show must go on, right?"

Even as it does when Bayern Munich play Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga's most marketed game this weekend, Kompany's absence will serve as a reminder that while much of the focus of modern sport is on the players, there is an equal level of support required for those on the sidelines.
